items.content: There is an explanation in the handbook in Section 4 to help you remember the diagram.

We are extending the context model to include the other person. We’ve drawn the diagram to show information flowing in a loop between the two people. It’s a simplification of what’s actually happening – think of it as a snapshot in time.
And, each person sees/hears, thinks/feels and says/does – they are sensing the situation and their reaction to that and responding to each other and the surroundings.
In a conversation each person brings their own context, makes meaning, makes assumptions and acts from that context.

This means we can make assumptions based on our own context, and forget the other person has a different context. So we might judge other people based on our context without realising we are doing that.
In this course we are asking you to be aware of what you are influencing and notice what might be happening for the other person (holding your assumptions lightly, of course!).
We think of this as creating a container for a better conversation. You might have a different metaphor for it.
We are going to do a couple of exercises now.
Point to the model where it says 'I see/hear' and 'they say/do' as you say this:
The first one helps you pay attention to what you see and hear them say and do.
Point to the model where it says 'I say/do' and 'their context' as you say this:
And the second exercise focuses on what you can be saying to find out more about their context.

Prepare BORs in 2/3s for 6 minutes if not already done.

Note that it is not recommended that this BOR timing is increased (unless there is a group of 3) as it is a listening only exercise.

items.content: For this first breakout exercise, you will have 6 minutes to practise listening to understand what the other person is saying and doing.
The exercise is going in the chat so it should travel to the breakout room with you. If you are on a mobile device, you might want to take a note of it in case you can’t see it.
Please share only what you feel comfortable sharing in the group when we come back into the main room.
Whilst you are listening, we would like to you to _avoid judging or interrupting the other person_.
Just to be clear, please do acknowledge each other with a nod or smile or “mmm”. However, don’t comment or ask any questions if you are listening.
Decide who is going to talk first. That person will talk about something that interests them (like a hobby or a pet), something that happened recently or what they might be doing after this session.
The other person or people will listen and pay close attention to what is said and done. Accept this without judgement or interruption.
Try noticing how the speaker is communicating through words, tone, and gestures.
Manage the time so everyone gets a chance to listen and be listened to.
We will send a message into the rooms to let you know when you are halfway through the time.
When you come back we will talk about what it’s like when you are talking to people who are listening well and what it’s like to be listening well.
Any questions before we send you in?

blocks.name: Unpack Breakout 1
blocks.speaker: fx2

items.content: You’ve practised paying attention to what the other person is saying or doing without judging or interrupting them. Listening to understand.
Now you are going to use questions to respond and extend your understanding of the other person’s context.
There are some questions going into the chat. These questions are constructed to remove assumptions and biases in the way you ask them.
They can quickly uncover someone’s thinking. We advise you don’t use more than two of these questions at a time to avoid the other person feeling like they are being interrogated!

We have seen the first two questions before in Module 2, where we used them to check our assumptions. These are: 
- What kind of ___ is that? 
- Is there anything else about that ___?

And we have got another for to ask about the meaning of something: 
- When you say___ I imagine___. Is that what you mean?

Sometimes, especially when someone seems to be stuck on a problem, it is useful to ask these questions about outcomes or next steps: 
- What would you like to have happen? 
- Then what happens?
We are going to do a quick demo
Facilitator to co-facilitator or producer to demo the questions:
And what are you doing today after the session?

Or any other easy question.

Ask one or two of the questions listed in the chat as a follow-up. If you can’t think what to say, ask the “Is there anything else about that?” question twice.
Copy to chat when the facilitator introduces the questions to the group:

To check assumptions:

- What kind of ___ is that? 
- Is there anything else about that ___? 

To ask about the meaning of something:

- When you say___ I imagine___. Is that what you mean? 

To ask about outcomes or next steps:

- What would you like to have happen?
- Then what happens?
Participate in the demo if there is no co-facilitator

If you can’t work out which question to use, you can ask “Is there anything else about that?” twice.
Remember, we are just practising here so it is a chance to try these questions out.
Manage the time so everyone has a chance to practise asking questions. Please only share what you are comfortable sharing.
We’ll talk about what it’s like to be asked these questions and to ask these questions when you come back.
